sections.html:
Property tax here is split between two elected offices: the Assessor, who decides values, and the Treasurer, who mails bills and takes payments. The county covers about 740 square miles, with the City of Boulder as its seat, and neighbors Larimer, Weld, Broomfield, Jefferson, Gilpin and Grand counties. It had 330,758 residents in 2020 and an estimated 328,560 in July 2025.

Cities and towns inside it include Boulder, Longmont, Lafayette, Louisville, Erie, Lyons, Nederland, Superior, Jamestown and Ward. They all bill through the same Treasurer, so a house in Lyons and a house in Lafayette share due dates.

Homes are valued high. The median owner-occupied home is worth $756,300, and 62.0% of homes are owner-occupied. Roughly 38% are rented, which means many sellers are landlords who also carry license and inspection costs in places like Boulder. At these values, even small rate changes shift a bill by hundreds of dollars.

The Colorado tax year opens on the January 1 assessment date and closes with the levies set in December.

  • January 1: assessment date for all taxable property, and the day the general tax lien attaches.
  • By May 1: Notices of Valuation for real property go out.
  • By June 8: real property appeals are filed.
  • August 25: the Assessor sends the Abstract of Assessment to the state and tells the taxing entities their values.
  • By December 15: local entities certify their levies.
  • By December 22: county commissioners levy the taxes.

Boulder County's own appeals page adds an August 15 determination date and a September 15 Board of Equalization deadline.

Each taxing body applies its own mill levy to the assessed value, and your bill adds those pieces together. Assessed value is actual value times the state's assessment rate.

Property type2025 rate2026 rate
Residential, school districts7.05%7.05%
Residential, local government6.25%6.8%
Commercial, industrial, vacant land, business personal property27%26%
Agricultural, renewable energy27%25%
Oil and gas production87.5%87.5%

For 2026, the local government side first subtracts 10% of the first $700,000 of a home's actual value. School district math skips that step. The Treasurer's account lookup shows the real figure for any address.

For 2026 the Treasurer listed March 2 and June 15 for half payments, or April 30 for the full amount. Send checks and money orders to the Boulder County Treasurer, and never mail cash.

A postmark sets the payment date. Interest on a first-half payment starts at 1% in March and reaches 6% by August. A full payment made in May costs 1% and reaches 4% by August. A second-half payment made June 16 to 30 costs 1% and reaches 3% in August.

For September through December, call the Treasurer. Payments after August 1 may carry extra fees.

The main Treasurer office sits on the first floor at 1325 Pearl St. in Boulder and keeps weekday hours of 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. A Longmont office at 515 Coffman St., Suite 113, opens on Mondays only.

  • Phone: 303-441-3520
  • Email: treasurer@bouldercounty.gov
  • Mail: P.O. Box 471, Boulder, CO 80306
  • The Lafayette office at 1755 S. Public Road is closed until late January 2027.

Phone the office to confirm how online payment works before you count on it.

Real property appeals are accepted from May 1 through June 8, and a late filing forfeits the right to appeal. File by email, mail, fax, online, drop box or in person at 1325 Pearl St., second floor.

A well-built appeal names the value you think is right, explains where the Assessor's figure goes wrong, and lists comparable sales by address, price and date. For this cycle the sales window runs July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2024, and if few sales exist, verified sales from up to five years earlier can be used.

You can also correct record errors, such as square footage, bedroom and bath count, lot size or basement finish. The Assessor's phone is 303-441-3530 and its email is assessor@bouldercounty.gov.

Once the Notice of Determination arrives, you can appeal in writing to the county Board of Equalization until September 15. After the board mails its decision there are 30 days left to choose among the State Board of Assessment Appeals, district court and binding arbitration. Business personal property appeals are filed June 15 to June 30.

Unpaid real property tax can be sold as a tax lien at the county's annual auction in November, and liens sold in 2026 carry 13% annual interest. The Treasurer posts the properties advertised for sale and updates the spreadsheet each Friday. Delinquent payments must be in certified funds.

To a seller, an unpaid balance is simply another closing item that the title company settles out of the sale. Colorado pays property tax in arrears, so a house sold in the spring may carry a bill for the prior year, and the January 1 lien date is why the closing agent checks the Treasurer's records.

On December 30, 2021 the Marshall Fire burned across 6,026 acres, destroying an estimated 1,084 structures and damaging 149. The September 2013 flood destroyed 262 homes in the county and damaged nearly 300. Anyone selling a house with that history should keep repair records, because buyer questions start there.

Once you accept an offer, the title company opens the file and asks the Treasurer where the account stands. It wants to know which halves are paid, whether interest has been added and whether the parcel appears on the advertised lien list. If a balance exists, it is paid from your proceeds, and the settlement statement shows the amount.

Timing matters because interest is added monthly. A closing pushed from one month into the next can change the payoff, so ask for an updated figure when the date moves. If you appealed your value, tell the buyer, since a lowered value affects the next bill, and hand over the Notice of Determination.

A cash buyer fits this process easily: no lender is checking the tax account, and the sale can close once the payoff and the deed are in order. Houses with deferred repairs, flood history or tenants are the cases where an as-is sale tends to save the most time. Whichever route you choose, write down who you spoke with at the county and what figure they quoted, so that a later question about the payoff has a paper trail behind it.

• Before choosing a closing date, request a payoff from the Treasurer.
  • Read your valuation notice as soon as it arrives in May, because the appeal window lasts only about five weeks.
  • Keep the Notice of Determination if you appealed, as it shows the value of record.

Deed recording runs $43 per document in this county, and the state's documentary fee of one cent per $100 over $500 comes on top.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal a Boulder County valuation?
faqs.a: June 8 is the last day for real property, up to 11:59 p.m. Late filings are not accepted.

faqs.q: When are Boulder County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Half payments are due March 2 and June 15, or the full amount April 30.

faqs.q: Who sets my Boulder County property value?
faqs.a: The county Assessor does, working from sales between July 1, 2022 and June 30, 2024. Setting the tax rate is not part of the job.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Boulder County tax bill itself?
faqs.a: No. Taxes are set by budgeting bodies such as county commissioners, city councils, school boards and special districts. You can appeal the value only.

faqs.q: How much interest applies if I pay late in Boulder County?
faqs.a: It depends on the month and the payment type. A full payment made in May carries 1%, while a first-half payment made in May carries 3%. For later months, call 303-441-3520.
